# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review of "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay" (Halden Institute WP 24-07)

The arithmetic in the paper is correct: the per-hour figures, the weighted means and the percentage changes all reproduce. The problems lie in what the numbers are taken to show. The headline claims (gains in output per hour in every sector, and a sector-general model) go well beyond the evidence, and in two places the paper's own data point the other way.

## 1. The "output per hour gain" is mostly arithmetic, not a finding

Output per scheduled hour is the output index divided by 0.8. Any sector whose output fell by less than 20% therefore shows a "gain" automatically.

- **Retail and hospitality:** output fell 6.9% (index 93.1). The paper reports this as a 16.4% *rise* in output per hour and calls it "notable". It is simply what dividing 93.1 by 0.8 gives.
- **"Consistency across sectors":** the claim that per-hour gains appeared in every sector is close to guaranteed by the method. It can't count as evidence of robustness.
- **The real test:** the pilot's own principle was "100% of the output". The question is whether the output index reached 100.
  - Only software (101.2) met it.
  - Overall output was 98.7, so it fell slightly.
  - Retail fell 6.9% and healthcare administration 3.5%.
- **The 23.4% figure is an upper bound.** It uses *scheduled* hours, and the authors concede (Limitation 4) that actual hours fell by less than 20% where staff worked extra. Output per *actual* hour could be considerably lower.

The honest headline is that output fell by about 1% overall, as reported by managers, and fell more in customer-facing sectors.

## 2. The paper's own data contradict "sector-general"

| Sector | Organisations | Reverted | Reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | **50%** |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 2 | **40%** |
| All other sectors | 50 | 0 | 0% |

- The two sectors with the lowest output are the only sectors where any organisation reverted.
- In those sectors, roughly half the organisations abandoned the schedule.
- The Discussion singles out retail as the strongest evidence for sector-generality. On these figures it is the strongest evidence *against* it.
- The samples are small: six retail organisations, and only those that volunteered.

## 3. Revenue doesn't support "no sign output was sacrificed"

- **Inflation.** The 1.4% is nominal growth over the prior year. With a pilot in 2023, when inflation in most advanced economies was several percent, this is likely a fall in *real* revenue. That is mildly negative evidence, not reassurance.
- **Missing reports.** Nine of the 61 organisations did not report revenue, and the reason isn't given. Non-reporting may correlate with poor results.
- **Scope mismatch.** Revenue is organisation-wide, but the intervention applied to "participating units". Where only some units took part, revenue is a diluted measure.
- **Inconsistent baselines.** Revenue is compared with the same months a year earlier, while output is compared with the preceding six months. The two series aren't comparable.

## 4. Seasonality is corrected for revenue but not elsewhere

The authors deseasonalised revenue but compared output, sick days and resignations with the six months immediately before the pilot.

- **Likely timing.** Recruitment was in early 2023 and was followed by two months of preparation. The baseline therefore probably covers late autumn to spring, including the winter illness season, and the pilot spring to autumn.
- **Effect on sickness.** A 36% fall in sick days from a winter-heavy baseline to a summer-heavy pilot period is largely what seasonality alone would produce.
- **Annualising.** Turning six months into annual rates amplifies the problem.
- **Resignations.** These also have seasonal patterns. During the pilot, staff had an obvious reason not to leave: they would lose a four-day week by moving elsewhere. That is a retention effect, but not evidence of better wellbeing or productivity.

## 5. The wellbeing evidence is weaker than presented

- **Energy is fading.** It rose 0.61 SD by month three but only 0.29 SD by month six, so more than half the gain disappeared within three months. That pattern fits a novelty or Hawthorne effect. It undercuts the "reduced fatigue" explanation and raises doubts about whether the gains last.
- **Survey details are missing.** Response rates at each wave aren't reported. Leavers are presumably absent from the month-six survey, which biases the comparison.
- **Self-rated productivity has no comparison.** The 64% "higher than before" figure has no baseline and no control. Employees who benefit from the scheme also have an obvious interest in its continuing.

## 6. The output measure is the weakest link, and the main result rests on it

- **Who rated it.** Managers rated output, and those same managers were responsible for the pilot.
- **No common standard.** Each organisation used "whatever output records the organisation held".
- **Anchoring.** A scale where 100 means "unchanged" invites reports clustered around 100.

This matters because, once the denominator artefact in section 1 is removed, the actual result is a −1.3% change in output. That is well within the range manager-reporting bias could produce. The authors say the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency". But the size and consistency come from the arithmetic, and the underlying effect is exactly the kind the limitations could overturn.

No dispersion is reported anywhere: no confidence intervals and no organisation-level distribution. A reader can't tell whether 98.7 reflects most organisations near 100 or a wide spread.

## 7. The causal story isn't supported

- **Fatigue versus process change.** The Discussion favours reduced fatigue as the main explanation. The manager interviews point instead to process changes: fewer meetings, focus blocks, simpler approvals and less reporting. 47 of 58 managers mentioned meetings.
- **Process changes don't need shorter hours.** If they drove the result, some of the benefit might be available without cutting hours. That bears directly on the policy recommendation.
- **No way to separate the two.** The design has no control group and no measure of fatigue's contribution. Neither explanation can be favoured on this evidence.

## 8. Selection, attrition and the continuation rate

- **Volunteers only.** Organisations volunteered and chose which units took part. The units most suited to reduced hours were probably the ones included.
- **Withdrawals.** Nine organisations withdrew before the pilot. They are likely to be those expecting difficulty, which inflates later success rates.
- **Continuation isn't productivity evidence.** The 92% figure comes from self-selected organisations, for whom reverting carries real costs in morale and retention. Only 18 of the 56 made the change permanent; the rest are presumably still trialling it.

## What the paper can support

On the evidence, the paper can claim the following:

- Among self-selected organisations, mostly in office and knowledge work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours coincided with a small reported fall in output (about 1%).
- Output fell more in customer-facing sectors (3–7%), and those sectors saw high reversion.
- Self-reported wellbeing improved, though the gains faded over time.
- Sickness and resignations fell, but the comparisons are confounded by seasonality.

**Specific revisions:**
- Remove "sector-general" and "gains in every sector" from the Summary and Discussion.
- Lead with the output index rather than output per scheduled hour, and present per-hour figures only alongside actual-hours data.
- Report real (inflation-adjusted) revenue and explain the nine missing reports.
- Use same-period-prior-year baselines for sick days and resignations, as was done for revenue.
- Report survey response rates, confidence intervals, and the organisation-level distribution of the output index.
- Discuss the retail and healthcare reversions as a substantive finding.
- Reframe "unlikely to overturn the main result": the limitations bear directly on the effect that remains once the arithmetic artefact is removed.

The recommendation that future pilots include a comparison group is the right one, and it deserves more prominence than it gets.
